purpose: Backstory pool for the sampling regime. A broad, researched history of immersive and visual media — the real shared past a divergent media-present can be grounded in. Lighter than the causal engine's events.json: no counterfactual outcomes or typed-state effects, just date, description, and thematic tags for backstory selection. Dates are established historical record; descriptions are the author's plain summaries. Expanded 2026-07-17 well beyond the 47-event causal vr-immersion theme.

tagLegend.immersion: envelopment, presence, filling the field of view/senses
tagLegend.image: still or moving pictorial image; visual fidelity
tagLegend.embodiment: the body as interface; movement, gesture, proprioception
tagLegend.wearable-body: worn on / carried on / inside the body
tagLegend.capital: commercial capital, venture funding, platform economics
tagLegend.gatekept-professional: produced by a professional caste or gatekept

events.label: Camera Obscura as Spectacle
events.description: The camera obscura, known since antiquity, becomes a room-scale attraction projecting the live outside world onto an interior wall — an early machine for putting a viewer inside an image.

events.label: The Magic Lantern
events.description: Christiaan Huygens and others develop the magic lantern, projecting painted glass slides to an audience — the ancestor of film projection and the first widely used image-projection medium.

events.label: Phantasmagoria
events.description: Étienne-Gaspard Robert stages horror shows using rear-projected magic lanterns on smoke, hidden screens, and sound effects to make ghosts seem to float in the room — immersion engineered to erase the medium.

events.label: Barker's Panorama
events.description: Robert Barker patents and exhibits the 360-degree panorama, a purpose-built rotunda whose wraparound painting surrounds the viewer with no visible edge — the first architecture of total visual immersion.

events.label: Brewster's Kaleidoscope
events.description: David Brewster's kaleidoscope becomes a runaway consumer craze — an early mass-market optical toy for private, handheld visual experience.

events.label: Daguerre's Diorama
events.description: Louis Daguerre opens the Diorama in Paris: huge translucent paintings transformed by changing light to animate scenes for a seated audience.

events.label: Phenakistoscope / Zoetrope
events.description: Plateau's phenakistoscope and later the zoetrope produce the illusion of motion from sequential drawings — the persistence-of-vision toys that made moving images a private, domestic pleasure.

events.label: The Daguerreotype
events.description: Photography goes public: the daguerreotype fixes an indexical image of the real, welding optical resemblance to causal trace — the assumption of fidelity that later media inherit.

events.label: Wheatstone's Stereoscope
events.description: Charles Wheatstone shows that feeding each eye a slightly different image yields a compelling depth illusion — the binocular principle every VR headset still uses.

events.label: Holmes's Handheld Stereoscope
events.description: Oliver Wendell Holmes designs a cheap, unpatented handheld stereoscope and deliberately leaves it open, making stereo viewing an inexpensive mass medium.

events.label: Stereoview Mass Culture
events.description: Card publishing and domestic adoption turn stereoscopic viewing into a normalized household medium — millions of stereo cards of travel, war, and novelty.

events.label: Muybridge's Motion Studies
events.description: Eadweard Muybridge's sequential photographs of a galloping horse prove photography can dissect motion — a step toward the moving image.

events.label: Ducos du Hauron's Anaglyph
events.description: Louis Ducos du Hauron patents the anaglyph, encoding a stereo pair in two colors viewed through colored glasses — 3D that could be projected to a group.

events.label: Edison's Kinetoscope
events.description: Dickson and Edison build the Kinetoscope, a peephole cabinet showing moving pictures to one paying viewer at a time — the moving image as private, coin-operated novelty.

events.label: Lumière Cinématographe
events.description: The Lumières project moving pictures to a paying audience, establishing collective theatrical cinema over Edison's private-viewing model.

events.label: Hale's Tours
events.description: Movie theaters built as replica train cars, rocking and playing forward-motion footage, give audiences an early immersive 'ride' cinema.

events.label: Theatrical Cinema Consolidates
events.description: Projection, distribution, and purpose-built theaters consolidate cinema into a durable, professionally produced mass institution.

events.label: The Power of Love (first 3D feature)
events.description: The first 3D feature film screens in anaglyph in Los Angeles — commercially inconsequential but proof of stereoscopic cinema.

events.label: Synchronized Sound / The Jazz Singer
events.description: Vitaphone and The Jazz Singer add synchronized recorded sound to film, ending the silent era and adding a whole sensory channel to the dominant medium.

events.label: Weinbaum's 'Pygmalion's Spectacles'
events.description: Stanley Weinbaum's science-fiction story imagines goggles delivering sight, sound, taste, smell, and touch of a fictional world — a strikingly complete prefiguration of VR.

events.label: The View-Master
events.description: The View-Master brings a held-to-the-face stereoscopic reel viewer to a mass consumer market, a direct ancestor of the head-mounted display.

events.label: Vitarama / Cinerama
events.description: Fred Waller's multi-projector panoramic systems culminate in Cinerama's curved 146-degree screen and stereo sound — immersion by widening the field of view.

events.label: The 3D Film Boom
events.description: Hollywood's first polarized-3D boom (Bwana Devil, House of Wax) briefly makes stereoscopic cinema mainstream before fading on cost and eyestrain.

events.label: CinemaScope / Widescreen
events.description: Anamorphic widescreen formats widen the frame as television threatens cinema — immersion as a competitive differentiator.

events.label: Heilig's 'Cinema of the Future'
events.description: Morton Heilig argues cinema must address all the senses, laying out a theory of multisensory immersive media decades ahead of the hardware.

events.label: Heilig's Sensorama
events.description: Heilig builds and patents the Sensorama, an arcade cabinet delivering stereo film, sound, wind, vibration, and smell — the first working multisensory immersive machine.

events.label: Heilig's Telesphere Mask
events.description: Heilig patents a head-mounted stereoscopic display with stereo sound, predating Sutherland's HMD.

events.label: Spacewar!
events.description: Students at MIT create Spacewar! on a PDP-1 — the first widely influential interactive computer game and a seed of interactive graphics.

events.label: Sutherland's Sketchpad
events.description: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad demonstrates interactive computer graphics with a light pen — the origin of the graphical, direct-manipulation interface.

events.label: Sutherland's 'The Ultimate Display'
events.description: Sutherland imagines a display that is a room in which the computer controls the existence of matter — the founding vision statement of virtual reality.

events.label: Engelbart's 'Mother of All Demos'
events.description: Douglas Engelbart demonstrates the mouse, hypertext, windows, and networked collaboration at once — augmenting the human intellect, funded by ARPA.

events.label: The Sword of Damocles
events.description: Sutherland and Bob Sproull build the first head-tracked, head-mounted computer display — heavy enough to hang from the ceiling — establishing computer-generated VR.

events.label: Krueger's Videoplace
events.description: Myron Krueger's camera-based Videoplace puts unencumbered bodies into a shared responsive graphic space — 'artificial reality' without goggles or gloves.

events.label: The Aspen Movie Map
events.description: MIT's Aspen Movie Map lets users navigate a town from filmed footage on videodisc — a surrogate-travel hypermedia precursor to Street View and virtual tourism.

events.label: Lucasfilm Computer Division
events.description: George Lucas hires Ed Catmull to build a computer graphics division, seeding the CGI pipeline that becomes Pixar and modern visual effects.

events.label: Home Video Game Console (Famicom/NES)
events.description: Nintendo's Famicom/NES makes interactive graphical worlds a fixture of the private home, training a mass audience in navigating simulated space.

events.label: NASA VIEW / DataGlove
events.description: NASA Ames builds the VIEW workstation pairing an HMD with a DataGlove for telepresence and simulation — assembling the modern VR rig.

events.label: VPL Research (EyePhone, DataGlove)
events.description: Jaron Lanier's VPL commercializes the EyePhone HMD and DataGlove and popularizes the term 'virtual reality' — the first VR company.

events.label: Nintendo Power Glove
events.description: Nintendo and Mattel's Power Glove brings a cheap gestural controller to living rooms; it fails commercially but seeds the idea of the body as a game interface.

events.label: The World Wide Web
events.description: Tim Berners-Lee proposes and releases the Web at CERN, an open hypertext system on the internet that becomes the dominant medium of networked distribution.

events.label: Virtuality VR Arcades
events.description: Virtuality installs networked stand-up VR arcade machines worldwide — the first mass commercial exposure to immersive VR gaming.

events.label: The CAVE
events.description: The University of Illinois CAVE projects stereo graphics on the walls of a room, an institutional, group-scale VR that needs no headset.

events.label: Sega VR / Nintendo Virtual Boy
events.description: Console makers' early consumer VR flops — Sega VR is shelved and Nintendo's Virtual Boy fails badly — chilling headset VR for a decade.

events.label: Char Davies's Osmose
events.description: Char Davies's Osmose uses breath and balance to navigate an ethereal VR world, reframing immersion as contemplative and bodily rather than heroic.

events.label: Toy Story
events.description: Pixar's Toy Story, the first fully computer-animated feature, proves synthetic imagery can carry mainstream narrative cinema.

events.label: Doom / Quake Real-Time 3D
events.description: id Software's Doom and Quake bring fast real-time 3D and networked multiplayer to the PC, building the engine lineage and modding culture VR later draws on.

events.label: Ultima Online / EverQuest (MMOs)
events.description: Persistent massively-multiplayer online worlds give thousands of people a shared, continuous virtual space to inhabit together.

events.label: Second Life
events.description: Linden Lab's Second Life offers a user-built, economy-bearing virtual world — an early 'metaverse' driven by amateur world-building rather than games.

events.label: Google Street View
events.description: Street View stitches panoramic photography into a navigable model of the real world — Aspen Movie Map at planetary scale.

events.label: Nintendo Wii
events.description: The Wii makes whole-body motion a mainstream game interface, reviving the body-as-controller idea for a mass market.

events.label: Microsoft Kinect
events.description: Kinect brings markerless full-body tracking to living rooms and becomes a widely hacked platform for embodied and research applications.

events.label: Oculus Rift Kickstarter
events.description: Palmer Luckey's Oculus Rift crowdfunds a cheap headset built from smartphone displays and inertial sensors, reigniting consumer VR.

events.label: Carmack Joins Oculus
events.description: Doom/Quake engineer John Carmack joins Oculus as CTO, lending the VR revival deep real-time-graphics credibility.

events.label: Facebook Acquires Oculus
events.description: Facebook buys Oculus for ~$2B, binding the future of consumer VR to a social-advertising platform rather than a gaming company.

events.label: Google Cardboard
events.description: A folded-cardboard smartphone holder makes the cheapest possible VR nearly free, briefly putting a headset in millions of hands.

events.label: Rift / Vive / PSVR Launch
events.description: Three room-scale consumer headsets launch within months, delivering tracked, hand-controllered VR at consumer prices for the first time.

events.label: Pokémon Go
events.description: Pokémon Go makes location-based augmented reality a global phenomenon, overlaying game objects on the physical world via the phone.

events.label: Beat Saber
events.description: Beat Saber becomes VR's breakout hit, showing that rhythmic full-body play, not simulation realism, is a native VR form.

events.label: Oculus Quest (Standalone VR)
events.description: The Quest cuts the PC cord, making self-contained, affordable headsets the mainstream form of consumer VR.

events.label: Half-Life: Alyx
events.description: Valve's Half-Life: Alyx is the first big-budget 'system-seller' VR game, demonstrating a mature immersive design vocabulary.

events.label: Facebook Becomes Meta / Horizon Worlds
events.description: Facebook rebrands as Meta and stakes its identity on the metaverse and Horizon Worlds, pouring tens of billions into social VR.

events.label: ChatGPT / Generative Text
events.description: ChatGPT makes large language models a mass medium, normalizing content produced on demand by a model rather than a person.

events.label: Diffusion Image Models (DALL·E 2, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney)
events.description: Text-to-image diffusion models decouple photorealism from indexicality — maximum resemblance with no camera — upending the assumption that images record the real.

events.label: Apple Vision Pro
events.description: Apple's $3,499 Vision Pro reframes the headset as 'spatial computing' with passthrough mixed reality, eye and hand tracking, and ultra-high visual fidelity.

events.label: Generative Video (Sora and peers)
events.description: Text-to-video models generate photorealistic moving footage from prompts, extending synthetic media from stills into time.

events.label: Generative World Models (Genie-class)
events.description: Genie-class systems generate interactive, navigable environments from a prompt or image — worlds produced by a model rather than authored or filmed.

events.label: World Labs / Spatial Intelligence
events.description: Fei-Fei Li's World Labs pursues 'spatial intelligence' — generating and reasoning over 3D worlds — merging the VR and generative-AI lineages.

events.label: Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal
events.description: Meta announces it will shut down the VR version of Horizon Worlds to pivot to AI, then reverses within days — a public wobble in the social-VR thesis.
